lead: Runtime defense, code approval and cross-request safety monitoring expose distinct enforcement and data-custody questions. A dated places benchmark makes grading limits visible; product rollouts, investment automation and legal reporting keep claims separate from verified outcomes.

sections.title: Runtime shields and static scanners protect different boundaries
sections.intro: A temporary Linux mitigation and a configuration scanner describe scoped defenses, not universal protection.

sections.title: Approval policies and zero retention describe different contracts
sections.intro: Claude Ship separates repair from approval; EFS moves storage custody without eliminating monitoring or costs.

sections.title: Local facts need dated keys and repeatable judgments
sections.intro: PlaceBench exposes its grading and repeat limits, while a chart alpha distinguishes suggestions from full-query aggregation.

sections.title: Unified workspaces are not permission to connect accounts
sections.intro: A demo inbox and a multi-pane IDE describe capabilities rather than tested privacy guarantees.

sections.title: Product rollouts and portfolios keep claims separate from outcomes
sections.intro: A reported model rollout, a satellite first close and an investing beta do not establish universal availability or performance.

sections.title: Prosecutors make allegations, not findings of guilt
sections.intro: Two reports about a former OpenAI engineer retain their separate access limits and distinguish a prosecution filing from adjudicated facts.

sections.title: Career anxiety is not a labor-market forecast
sections.intro: An Ask HN thread brings conflicting personal views, not a representative estimate of which jobs automation will change.
